t: Minimum Number of Operations to Convert Time — Greedy on Coin Denominations
o: Both times are converted to minutes since midnight; because current <= correct is guaranteed, the target is a non-negative difference d of at most 1439 minutes, and no day wraparound ever happens. In Example 1, d = 04:35 - 02:30 = 125 minutes, solved optimally as two 60-minute jumps plus one 5-minute jump = 3 operations. In Example 2, d = 1 needs a single 1-minute operation. The allowed increments {60, 15, 5, 1} form a coin system where each denomination divides the next larger one, so the minimum operation count has both a simple greedy solution and a general coin-change DP fallback.
k: Parse HH:MM into absolute minutes; the task reduces to representing d = target - current as a sum of coins from {60, 15, 5, 1} with fewest coins.
Each step divides the next larger one (1 | 5 | 15 | 60), so greedily consuming the largest step first is provably optimal.
d < 1440, so an O(d) dynamic program over minute values is also comfortably fast and generalizes to arbitrary step sets.

a.i: Treat the increments as coins and d as the amount: dp[x] is the fewest operations to build exactly x minutes. Each state tries all four coins, guaranteeing correctness regardless of the coin system's structure. It is the most universally applicable way to think about the problem, though slightly more code and memory than needed here.
s: Convert both times to minutes and compute d.
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[x] = infinity for x > 0.
For x from 1 to d, set dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - step]) over all steps <= x.
a.t: O(d) — up to 1440 states, each trying 4 coins.
a.sp: O(d) — one DP entry per possible minute difference.

a.i: Take as many 60s as possible, then 15s, then 5s, then 1s. Optimality follows from the divisibility chain: any optimal solution's remainder handling can be exchanged into larger coins without raising the count (e.g., five 1s trade for one 5). Since d < 1440 the arithmetic is tiny, giving constant time and space — the ideal interview answer.
s: Convert both times to minutes and compute d.
For each step in [60, 15, 5, 1]: add d // step to the answer and set d %= step.
a.t: O(1) — four divisions after constant-time parsing.

w: Present greedy first (it is optimal here thanks to the canonical denominations) and offer the DP as the safety net if the interviewer changes the step set to something non-canonical like {60, 25, 10, 1}, where plain greedy can be beaten. Pitfalls: forgetting that current <= correct removes wraparound logic entirely, and mis-parsing 'HH:MM' substrings (index 3 onward holds MM). Edge cases include equal times (answer 0) and differences needing only 1s. A natural follow-up asks the same question when the time may wrap past midnight, turning d into (target - current + 1440) % 1440.
